sources.title: Intermittent fasting vs. calorie restriction: which actually ...
sources.snippet: Sep 7, 2026 · A 2023 meta-analysis in Nutrients of seven randomized trials with 458 participants found that time-restricted eating combined with a calorie deficit produced 2.11 kg more weight loss than calorie restriction alone. Improvements in blood glucose and lipids, however, came primarily from the calorie deficit itself, not the timing.

answer:
The evidence is mixed. One randomized trial in *Annals of Internal Medicine* found that a 4:3 fasting schedule outperformed daily calorie restriction: after one year, the fasting group lost an average of about 6 more pounds [6]. Another report of the same study says the fasting group lost 2.89 kg more, a statistically significant but clinically modest edge, and lost 7.6 percent of body weight versus 5.0 percent with daily restriction [6].

However, other research shows comparable results. A 2026 *Clinical Nutrition* trial found intermittent fasting and continuous calorie restriction produced comparable weight loss when calories were matched; the calorie-restriction-only group lost 6.3 kg and the difference of 1.8 kg was not statistically significant [3]. A 2025 meta-analysis also reported a "slightly greater, though statistically nonsignificant, weight decrease" for intermittent fasting [6].

Overall, the sources do not say fasting always leads to more weight loss. Some meta-analyses found small advantages for fasting: a 2023 analysis of time-restricted eating plus calorie deficit found 2.11 kg more weight loss than calorie restriction alone [6], and a 2022 analysis reported a small but significant advantage for fasting, with essentially identical BMI outcomes [6]. The possible edge may come from adherence rather than physiology: some people find fasting easier to stick to [3].
